findings.description: The EC2 user_data script embeds long-lived AWS access key ID and secret access key (AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMAAA / wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMAAAKEY) in plaintext. User data is retrievable from the instance metadata service by any process or SSRF vector on the host, and the credentials are also stored in Terraform state, so the keys can be harvested and used to access the account.

The security group allows TCP/22 (SSH) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing administrative access of the public web host to the entire internet and permitting brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks. TCP/80 is also open to 0.0.0.0/0, but SSH exposure is the material risk.

The EBS volume attached to the portal server is created without `encrypted = true`, so data written by the Apache host is stored unencrypted and is readable by anyone who obtains the underlying volume or its snapshot.

The snapshot is taken from an unencrypted EBS volume and does not set `encrypted`, so the backup retains the plaintext contents of the server disk and can be copied or shared without encryption protections.
The bucket storing VPC flow logs is defined with no server-side encryption configuration, so network metadata (source/destination IPs, ports, and traffic patterns) is stored unencrypted at rest.

`map_public_ip_on_launch = true` causes every instance launched in this subnet, including the portal server, to receive a publicly routable IP by default, expanding the internet-facing attack surface beyond instances that genuinely require one.
`map_public_ip_on_launch = true` makes this subnet auto-assign public IP addresses to all launched instances, exposing them directly to the internet without an explicit opt-in per workload.
